fixes.explanation: No famine here, friend. Nothing in this passage mentions one. Phinehas says, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him. Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.” The rescue he names is from the hand of the LORD, and that's the one to remember.

The text never says anyone tears it down. After the report, the Israelites “…blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them…” The altar ends the passage with a name instead. The Reubenites and Gadites say, “It is a witness between us that the LORD is God.”

That's it, baker. Joshua points them to what Moses, the servant of the LORD, gave them: “to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” Loving the LORD and holding fast to Him are both right there in the list. That's two of the five things Joshua names.

An altar, friend. The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh build an imposing one at Geliloth, right by the Jordan. Imposing is the text's own word for it. Keep an eye on that altar, because it's about to cause a stir.

The report puts the altar somewhere else. It says they built it “…on the border of the land of Canaan, at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side.” That's the Canaan side of the river, not out in Gilead. So the statement is false, and the report itself says where the altar sits.

The plan at Shiloh is war, not blessing. When they heard the report, the whole congregation assembled there to go to war against the three tribes. Israel does bless God later in the chapter, once the report comes back (Joshua 22:33). That's a different moment from this gathering.

Sharing the spoil comes from Joshua's farewell, when he tells the three tribes to divide the spoil of their enemies with their brothers (Joshua 22:8). The gathering at Shiloh is about something else. After hearing the report, the whole congregation assembles to go to war against them. Different scene, different plan.

That's right. The text says Israel sent ten chiefs, “…one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel.” Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, goes with them. So every tribe of Israel has a family leader in that group.

Close, because war is on the table. But the text describes the ten chiefs this way: “…one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel.” Army captains aren't how the verse describes them. Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, goes along with them.

The verse calls the ten chiefs “…one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel.” That's family leaders, not priests. Phinehas is the one the text names as son of Eleazar the priest. So the ten are clan heads, one from each tribe.

That's how the delegation puts it. They ask, “What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel by turning away from the LORD and building for yourselves an altar…” A little later they ask, “And now, would you turn away from the LORD?” That's a serious charge to bring to their own brothers.

The offer goes the other way. The leaders say to cross over to the land where the LORD’s tabernacle stands. Then they add, “…do not rebel against the LORD or against us by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God.” So a second altar is what they warn against, and a tabernacle of their own never comes up.

Joshua did tell them earlier that they had not deserted their brothers (Joshua 22:3), but that was his praise, not their fear. The fear they name here is different. They say descendants might tell theirs, “You have no share in the LORD!”

A witness, baker. They say, “…let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come, that we will worship the LORD in His presence…” It's meant to keep speaking long after everyone in this conversation is gone. A bit like a photo on the fridge, telling the story to whoever walks by.

That's what they'd point to. They say they would answer, “Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you.” So it's a copy and not a rival. Pointing at something people can see beats a long speech any day.

They were. The text says that when Phinehas the priest and the chiefs heard what the descendants of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh had to say, “…they were satisfied.” They had come with a hard question, and the answer they got was enough for them. I bet those chiefs felt a lot lighter on the walk back.

The text says the opposite. When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs heard what the descendants of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh had to say, “…they were satisfied.” So the answer from the three tribes was enough for them. Satisfied is the word the text uses.
